newsitem.title: USA: U.S. sending some 30 jet fighters to Qatar.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sending some 30 jet fighters to Qatar.

text.p: The United States will send about 30 F-15E and F-16 fighter jets to Qatar this month in a temporary deployment to show U.S. commitment to protecting moderate Gulf states, the Pentagon said on Thursday.
Qatari and U.S. officials said in Doha earlier that the move was being made after consultation between the two countries and that the jets would remain in Qatar from Feb. 20 to May 20.

The Defence Department said the so-called airpower expeditionary force would include F-15Es from Seymour Johnson Air Force Base in North Carolina and F-16s from three bases in South Carolina and New Mexico.
The planes are designed for ground attack and aerial combat with other jets and will temporarily join some 200 U.S. jets permanently stationed in the Gulf region as a buffer against Iraq and Iran.

Pentagon officials said the deployment was intended to improve long-term military relations with Qatar, enhance joint training and fly U.S. missions in support of "Operation Southern Watch" over Iraq.
This enforces a no-fly zone over southern Iraq declared by the United States and other Western powers in 1992.
It will be the second deployment of the U.S. Airpower Expeditionary Force to Qatar since last year. Some 34 aircraft were deployed in Qatar from July 3 to Sept. 2.
The United States has also sent groups of fighters to other states in the Middle East, including Bahrain and Jordan, on a temporary basis.
The Air Force said the F-16s would deploy to Qatar from McIntyre Air National Guard Base and Shaw Air Force Base in South Carolina and from Cannon Air Force Base in New Mexico.
Oil and gas-rich Qatar signed a defence treaty with the United States after the 1991 Gulf War which liberated Kuwait from Iraqi occupation.
Qatar, a peninsula on the east coast of Saudi Arabia, is the site of two U.S. military warehouses where heavy armour is being stationed for possible emergency use by U.S. ground forces.
Last year, the navies and air forces of the two countries held three sets of exercises to train for what they described as "any eventuality."
